sections.title: The General Principle of the Laws of Mixtures
sections.html:
There are two fundamental rules in the law of forbidden foods that became mixed with permitted foods. The first rule: bitul be-shishim (nullification in sixty): if the forbidden substance became mixed into a quantity whose volume is sixty times greater than it, its flavor is not perceptible, and the mixture is permitted to eat. For this is how the Sages estimated: if the permitted food contains sixty times the forbidden substance, it is known that the flavor of the forbidden substance is nullified, because even foods with a very strong flavor, such as onion, do not impart flavor in more than sixty times their amount (Ḥullin 97b, Ran and Ra'avya).

The second rule: bitul be-rov (nullification in a majority): if the forbidden food does not impart flavor to the mixture – one follows the majority. For example, a piece of tereifa meat that became mixed with two pieces of kosher meat like it – it is nullified in the majority, as it is stated (Shemot 23:2): “Incline after the majority” (SA 109:1; below section 8).

For the forbidden substance to impart flavor to the permitted food, two conditions must be met: first, that the mixture be min be-she'eino mino (a kind with a different kind), that is, that the flavor of the forbidden substance is different from the flavor of the permitted food, so that it can be perceived in it. Second, that the mixture be laḥ be-laḥ (liquid with liquid), for then the flavor of the forbidden substance blends into the mixture. For example: when milk becomes mixed into a meat soup, its flavor spreads through the soup. Likewise, when a piece of non-kosher meat is cooked with vegetables, the non-kosher flavor mixes into the vegetables.

But if one of the two conditions is not met, even though the forbidden and the permitted are mixed, the flavor of the forbidden substance does not spread into the permitted food. For example, if a piece of forbidden meat became mixed with two pieces of permitted meat whose flavor is different, even though this is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino, since the mixture is yavesh be-yavesh (dry with dry), the flavor of the forbidden substance does not pass into the permitted foods, and therefore by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority. Likewise, when gravy of tereifa meat became mixed with gravy of kosher meat, even though the mixture is laḥ be-laḥ and the forbidden substance blends into the permitted, since the flavor of the forbidden substance is like the flavor of the permitted, it does not impart flavor to it, and therefore by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority.

However, the Sages made a protective fence for the Torah and enacted that even when only one of the two conditions that enable the transfer of flavors is met – either it is a mixture of laḥ be-laḥ, or it is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino – the forbidden substance is not nullified in a majority, but sixty times is needed to nullify it (Rashba and Rosh). The Sages had another important aim in their enactment: to make the measures uniform, so that there would be a single law of nullification in sixty for all mixtures that resemble a mixture in which the forbidden substance can impart flavor (Ran). Therefore, even when the basis of the prohibition is rabbinic, we do not say that there is no need to make a fence for it; rather, sixty times is needed to nullify it, because the Sages made their measures uniform (Beit Yosef and Rema 109:1).1

sections.title: Summary of the Four Types of Mixtures
sections.html:
Thus there are two distinctions in the laws of mixtures: the first, min be-mino (a kind with its own kind) and min be-she'eino mino. In min be-mino the flavor of the forbidden substance is the same as the flavor of the permitted; in min be-she'eino mino the flavor of the forbidden substance is different from the flavor of the permitted.

The second: laḥ be-laḥ and yavesh be-yavesh. In laḥ be-laḥ the flavor of the forbidden substance blends into the mixture, such as non-kosher meat cooked with kosher meat, where through the cooking the flavors mix throughout the dish. Forbidden flour that became mixed with permitted flour is also considered a mixture of laḥ be-laḥ, since flour is fine and the forbidden and permitted particles blend into one another (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 7:4). By contrast, in a mixture of yavesh be-yavesh we do not know which food is kosher and which is forbidden, but they do not blend into one another. A cup containing gravy of non-kosher meat that became mixed up with two cups containing gravy of kosher meat is also considered a mixture of yavesh be-yavesh, because the gravies are in separate cups and do not mix with one another.

Since the two distinctions combine with each other, there are four types of mixtures: a) min be-she'eino mino, laḥ be-laḥ; b) min be-she'eino mino, yavesh be-yavesh; c) min be-mino, laḥ be-laḥ; d) min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh.

In the first three types, sixty times is needed to nullify the forbidden substance. In the first, sixty times is needed by the essential law, because of the flavor the forbidden substance imparts to the mixture. In the second and third types, by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority, and the Sages enacted that it is not nullified in less than sixty. Only in a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh) is the practical halakha that the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority. Admittedly, some hold that the Sages made all the measures uniform and established that no forbidden substance is nullified in less than sixty times. However, in practice the halakha follows the opinion of most Rishonim, that a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh) is nullified in a majority, and this is the situation in which the fundamental rule of nullification in a majority applies.

However, specifically regarding a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh), when the prohibition has extra severity, the Sages were more stringent than with other mixtures, which are nullified in sixty. If the forbidden substance is teruma fruit that became mixed with ordinary fruit, since the prohibition of teruma has extra severity – a non-kohen who eats it is punishable by death [at the hands of Heaven] – the teruma fruit is nullified only if the ḥullin (non-sacred) fruit is a hundred times as much. And when the forbidden substance is orla fruit or kilei ha-kerem (mixed vineyard produce), which are forbidden even for benefit, the forbidden substance is nullified only if the permitted fruit is two hundred times as much (below, halakha 9).2

sections.title: Ta'am Ke-ikar and Nullification in Sixty
sections.html:
As we have learned, in any situation in which the flavor of the forbidden substance can be perceived in the mixture, the entire mixture is forbidden, because ta'am ke-ikar (“flavor is like the substance itself”). That is, the flavor of a food is considered like its substance. Therefore, even when the forbidden substance is small in quantity, and the permitted flavors are many and stronger than it, as long as the flavor of the forbidden substance is perceptible – the forbidden substance is not nullified in the mixture, and all of it is forbidden to eat. The Sages estimated that the flavors of all foods are nullified in sixty, because even foods whose flavor is strong, such as onion, impart flavor up to sixty times and no more. Therefore the Sages established that all forbidden substances that can impart flavor are nullified in sixty. The exception is spices, whose flavor is strong, and the permitted food must contain a much larger amount in order to nullify their flavor (below section 6).

Therefore, if a little milk fell into a meat soup, and the soup did not contain sixty times the milk – the soup is forbidden. And if the soup contained sixty times the milk, it is clear to us that the flavor of the milk is not perceptible and the soup is kosher. Everything cooking in the soup combines to nullify the milk that fell into it in sixty, including: meat, vegetables, water and bones. Even bones that have no flavor, since they too absorb the flavors in the dish, also combine toward the measure of sixty times with which the forbidden substance is nullified (SA 99:1).

Likewise, if a little ground non-kosher meat became mixed into vegetable patties, if the vegetables contain sixty times the meat, it is known that the flavor of the meat is nullified and the patties are kosher. And if there is not sixty times – the patties are forbidden. Likewise, if non-kosher meat fell into a vegetable soup, if the soup contained sixty times against it, the soup is kosher; however, since it is possible to remove the non-kosher meat, one must remove it, for as long as it is recognizable – only its flavor is nullified, while it itself is not nullified. And if the soup did not contain sixty times against it, even though the non-kosher meat is removed, since its flavor spread through the soup and there was not sixty times against it – the entire soup is forbidden.3

sections.title: Tasting by a Gentile
sections.html:
Although we have learned that as a rule the forbidden substance is nullified in sixty, when it is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino, since the forbidden substance has a flavor different from the permitted, one may give a gentile the dish to taste. If he perceives the flavor of the forbidden substance – the dish is forbidden; and if he does not perceive it, even though the permitted food does not contain sixty times – the dish is permitted (Ḥullin 97a-b). For we have learned that the reason the Sages enacted that forbidden substances be nullified in sixty is that even foods whose flavor is strong, such as onion, impart flavor up to sixty times and no more. Thus foods whose flavor is less strong are nullified in less than sixty times. But as long as we have no way of checking this, the Sages enacted that the forbidden substance be nullified in sixty; but if a reliable gentile says that there is no forbidden flavor in the mixture, the food is kosher.

Admittedly, many are stringent and hold that even when it is not possible to perceive the flavor of the forbidden substance, whenever there is not sixty times against the actual substance of the forbidden item, the mixture is forbidden (Ramban, Rashba, Ra'ah and Ran). But in practice the ruling follows the opinion of those who hold that even when actual forbidden substance became mixed into kosher food, if a reliable gentile said that the food has no forbidden flavor, even though the permitted food does not contain sixty times against the forbidden substance, the mixture is kosher, because everything depends on flavor (Rambam, Tosafot, Rosh, Tur and SA 98:1).

Therefore, if milk fell into a meat dish, the gentile should taste the dish. If he perceives a dairy flavor in it – the dish is forbidden. And if he does not perceive it, even though the meat dish does not contain sixty times the milk – the dish is permitted. Likewise, if non-kosher meat fell into a vegetable dish, the gentile should taste the dish; if he perceives a meat flavor in it – the dish is forbidden. And if he does not perceive it, even though the dish does not contain sixty times the non-kosher meat – the dish is kosher.

However, the problem is that the gentile may deviate from the truth in order to please the Jew or to harm him; therefore they said that only if he speaks innocently (mesi'aḥ lefi tumo), that is, he does not know that his answer has halakhic significance, may one rely on him. And if he is a cook, one may tell him that it concerns a halakhic question, and since his profession requires discerning flavors, he will give an accurate answer so as not to harm his professional reliability (Rashba).4

sections.title: The Practical Custom – Nullification in Sixty
sections.html:
Several of the great Rishonim in Ashkenaz wrote that the practical custom is not to rely on tasting by a gentile; rather, if the permitted food contains sixty times more than the forbidden substance – the mixture is kosher, and if it does not contain sixty times – the mixture is forbidden. Apparently, the poskim found that in practice it is difficult to rely on tasting the dish, because flavor is elusive, and at times it happened that a gentile answered that the dish had no meat flavor, and when the Jew ate from it, he found that it had a meat flavor. And at times there were people who perceived the forbidden flavor and people who did not perceive it. The definition of flavor is also unclear: whether it refers to perceiving the flavor of the forbidden substance itself, or also to a different flavor having been created in the dish as a result of the forbidden substance. Therefore some of the Rishonim ruled not to rely on tasting by a gentile, but rather that all forbidden substances be nullified in sixty. Over the years this custom spread to all communities, until in recent generations all Israel are accustomed to rely on nullification in sixty and not on tasting by a gentile (Rema 98:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2; 11).

However, in a pressing situation, when a reliable gentile says with complete certainty that the dish has no forbidden flavor, one may permit the dish.5

sections.title: Spices and Coagulants
sections.html:
A spice imparts flavor in more than sixty times its amount; therefore, if a forbidden spice became mixed into a food, as long as its flavor is perceptible it renders the entire food forbidden, even if the food is a thousand times greater than it or more (Rema 98:8).6

Regarding a forbidden substance that causes the mixture to change its form or its nature, the Sages were stringent and established that even if there is sixty times against it, it is not nullified, since its effect is evident in the mixture. Therefore, if the stomach lining of a nevela was placed in milk so that the enzymes in it would turn the milk into cheese, the cheese is forbidden, since it was curdled by means of nevela (above 30:6). Likewise, if dough was leavened with forbidden yeast, the dough is forbidden even if it contained sixty times against the yeast. Likewise, if by means of forbidden yeast or vinegar a honey drink or fruit drink was fermented and turned into an intoxicating beverage, the beverage is forbidden even if it contained sixty times against the yeast (SA and Rema 87:11).

If the forbidden substance did not have enough to impart flavor to the food or to curdle it, and only with the help of a permitted flavor or a permitted coagulant did it impart flavor to the food or curdle it – its law is like that of other forbidden substances, and whenever the food contains sixty times against the forbidden substance – the food is kosher (Rema ibid.). This rule is called: “zeh ve-zeh gorem (this and that both cause it) – it is permitted.”7

sections.title: Noten Ta'am Li-fgam Is Permitted
sections.html:
A forbidden food that fell into a dish and spoiled its flavor – even though the dish does not contain sixty times against the forbidden substance, and the flavor of the forbidden substance is noticeable in the dish – since its flavor spoils the dish, it is nullified in a majority and does not render the dish forbidden, in accordance with the rule: “noten ta'am li-fgam (one that imparts a detrimental flavor) – is permitted.” And even when the forbidden substance itself is tasty, as long as it spoils the dish, the dish is permitted. The spoilage need not be such that because of it people would refrain from eating the dish; rather, whenever the forbidden substance spoiled the flavor of the dish – the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority and the dish is permitted. But if the forbidden substance neither spoiled the flavor of the dish nor improved it, as long as its flavor is noticeable, the dish is forbidden (Avoda Zara 67b; SA 103:1-2).

Some say that even when the forbidden substance adds to the quantity of the dish, to the point that the gain from the increased quantity exceeds the loss from the spoiling of the flavor, the dish is permitted. For the main thing is the flavor, and as long as the forbidden substance spoils the flavor of the dish, it is nullified in a majority (Rashba). And some say that since in practice there is a benefit from the forbidden substance that became mixed into the dish – the dish is forbidden (Ran). In practice, one should be stringent, and in a pressing situation one may be lenient (see SA 103:2; Ziv'ḥei Tzedek 12).

Noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted on condition that the forbidden food always imparted a detrimental flavor; but if at first it improved and afterwards spoiled, or at first spoiled and afterwards improved – it is forbidden (SA 103:2).8

sections.title: The Law of Dry with Dry, Same Kind
sections.html:
As we have learned (in halakha 2), a piece of tereifa meat that became mixed with two pieces of kosher meat whose flavor is the same – the tereifa piece is nullified in the majority of kosher pieces. The same law applies when five forbidden pieces became mixed with six permitted pieces like them: since the majority is permitted, the minority is nullified and the entire mixture is kosher (SA 109:1; Shakh 6).

And although by Torah law the forbidden piece was nullified in the majority and became like a permitted one, by rabbinic law it is forbidden to eat all the pieces together, for if one eats them together, it is clear that with each and every eating he will also eat of the forbidden substance; rather, he should eat piece after piece, and in this way with each and every eating he can say that he is not eating of the forbidden substance. Likewise, it is forbidden to cook all the pieces together, because the cooking mixes the flavors of all the pieces, so that with every eating he will be eating of all of them (Rashba). And some say that by rabbinic law it is forbidden for one person to eat all the pieces, even one after another; rather, it is permitted only for two people to eat them, and in this way each one can say that he himself did not eat of the forbidden substance (Semag). Le-khatḥila it is good to be stringent in accordance with this view.9

sections.title: Things That Are Not Nullified in Sixty
sections.html:
All that we have learned, that forbidden substances are nullified in sixty, and sometimes in a majority, applies specifically to ordinary forbidden substances; but with forbidden substances that have an aspect of severity, the Sages were more stringent. There are forbidden substances regarding which the Sages were stringent that they not be nullified even in a thousand, and there are forbidden substances regarding which the Sages were stringent that they be nullified in a measure of a hundred or two hundred. We will learn the laws from the most severe to the most lenient:

The basis for forbidden substances being nullified in sixty is that relative to such a large quantity of permitted food, the forbidden substance is nullified by virtue of its extreme smallness, as evidenced by the fact that even its flavor is not noticeable in a quantity sixty times greater than it. But when the forbidden substance has extra severity or significance, even in a very large mixture its name is noticeable, and in a person's awareness it is not nullified. Therefore the Sages enacted that especially significant things are not nullified even in a thousand, and they are:
a) a beriya (a whole creature) (below section 10); b) a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed bah (a piece fit to serve to an honored guest) (below section 11); c) significant items that are counted (below section 12). All these forbidden substances are not nullified, whether they became mixed with their own kind or with a different kind.

They further enacted that ḥametz on Pesaḥ and the prohibition of idolatry, because of their extra severity, are not nullified even in a thousand, whether with their own kind or with a different kind (SA OḤ 447:1; YD 140:1; Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 7:1-2).

Forbidden spices render their mixture forbidden as long as their flavor is noticeable. Likewise, something that curdles the food is not nullified as long as its effect is noticeable (above halakha 6).

And there are two types of forbidden substances regarding which the Sages enacted that only if they became mixed with a different kind are they nullified in sixty, but if they become mixed with their own kind, they are not nullified even in a thousand. They are: a) davar she-yesh lo matirin (something that will become permitted) (below section 14); b) the wine of gentiles, regarding which there is a concern that it was poured as a libation for idolatry (SA 134:2-3).

And there are forbidden substances that, if they became mixed with a different kind, are nullified in sixty, but if they became mixed with their own kind, since they have a certain severity, are not nullified in sixty but rather in a higher measure. They are: teruma and ḥalla, orla and kilei ha-kerem. The severity of teruma and ḥalla is that one who eats them intentionally is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (above 7, note 10), and therefore the Sages were stringent that they be nullified in a hundred (Mishna Ḥalla 1:9). Their nullification is in a hundred because terumat ma'aser, which renders the produce fit, is one hundredth, and the Sages taught that if it falls back into the ninety-nine parts that remained, it is not nullified, and one would need to treat all the produce according to the law of teruma; but if it falls into a hundred – it is nullified, and the produce is permitted to be eaten by all Israel (except that one must give the kohen the amount of the teruma that fell, since this portion belongs to him).

With orla and kilei ha-kerem the punishment is indeed ordinary (lashes), but their prohibition is more severe, for they are forbidden both for eating and for benefit; therefore the Sages enacted that they be nullified in a double measure – in two hundred (Mishna Orla 2:1; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:13-16).10

sections.title: Beriya
sections.html:
The Sages enacted that a beriya (a whole creature), such as a worm, is not nullified even in a thousand. Specifically the beriya itself is not nullified, but its flavor is nullified in sixty (Ḥullin 100a). This principle, that a beriya has significance, we learned from the prohibition of eating insects: generally only one who eats a volume of a kezayit of the forbidden substance is punished with lashes, but when the forbidden substance is a beriya, such as an insect, even when it is smaller than a kezayit, one who eats it is punished with lashes (above 23:1).

Four conditions must be met for a forbidden substance to be considered a beriya and not be nullified even in a thousand: a) It must be from the animal kingdom and not the plant kingdom; therefore a grain of wheat does not have the status of a beriya. b) The beriya must be whole; but if part of it was cut off, such as a leg, or it was crushed until its form changed – it does not have the significance of a beriya. c) A whole limb of an animal can also have the status of a beriya, if it has a distinct name and if it were divided – its name would be lost. Therefore the gid ha-nasheh (sciatic nerve) and ever min ha-ḥai (a limb from a living animal) have the status of a beriya, but ḥelev does not have the status of a beriya, because even if it is cut, its name remains ḥelev. d) The status of beriya exists only when the forbidden substance was forbidden from its inception, such as an insect, the gid ha-nasheh or a non-kosher bird; but a kosher bird that died without ritual slaughter does not have the status of a beriya, because its prohibition is not intrinsic, but rather because it died without kosher slaughter (SA 100:1; above 23:4).11

sections.title: Significant Items
sections.html:
Foods that are so especially significant that, because of their great significance, people always count them one by one, are not nullified. The Sages gave examples of this: a special pomegranate called the “pomegranate of Badan” (from Bidan near Elon Moreh), or a special nut called the “nut of Perekh” (from Purikh near Shekhem), large and special cabbage stalks, a large sealed barrel of wine, and likewise anything that is always customarily sold by count because of its significance. But things sold by weight or volume are nullified like other forbidden substances. Likewise, things that are customarily sold by count for the purpose of calculating their price and not because of their significance, such as packages of rice and sugar, cans of preserves and bottles of wine – are nullified like other forbidden substances. An example of a significant item in our day is an especially high-quality bottle of wine or whisky whose price is hundreds of shekels.12

All that the Sages ruled to be stringent regarding significant items, a beriya and a piece fit to serve to an honored guest – that they are not nullified even in a thousand – applies when the mixture remains as it was, for then, because of the significance of the forbidden substance, it is not nullified. But if one of the items in the mixture fell into the sea or became mixed into a non-kosher dish, in a manner that there is no longer any possibility that a Jew will ever eat it, we attribute it, saying that perhaps it was the forbidden item that fell and was lost, and consequently the forbidden substance no longer has extra significance, and it is nullified according to the accepted rules, in a majority or in sixty. However, the Sages added a condition to the permission: that each time one eats from the mixture, he eat two pieces together, and if they are large, that with each eating he eat from both of them together, so that there will always be certainty that one of the pieces he is eating is permitted, and then its companion is drawn after it (Zevaḥim 74a; SA 110:7).13

sections.title: A Piece Fit to Serve to an Honored Guest
sections.html:
The Sages established that a piece fit to serve to an honored guest is not nullified even in a thousand, because owing to its great significance, even when it is mixed in sixty it is not nullified in a person's awareness. A piece fit to serve to an honored guest is a piece that can be served to an honored guest as the main part of the meal, so that he will be satisfied from it together with bread or rice and the like. Everything depends on the time and place: there were periods when people customarily honored a guest with a medium piece of meat or a medium piece of hard cheese, because they would then eat a lot of bread with the meat or the cheese, and together with the bread they were customarily satisfied by them. But in our day, when food is more abundant, a piece fit to serve to an honored guest must be at least a quarter of a large chicken, or beef of that size. And when there is a doubt whether the piece is fit to serve to an honored guest, since this law is rabbinic, one is lenient and treats it like other forbidden substances.14

Some say that only a piece that can be served to a guest as it is, is considered fit to serve to an honored guest; but if its cooking was not completed, or it is too large, its law is like that of other forbidden substances (Ran; SA 101:3). And although many Rishonim and Aḥaronim are stringent even while it is raw and large, since the basis of this law is rabbinic, in a pressing situation one may rely on the lenient opinions.15

Even when the piece is forbidden by rabbinic law, if it is fit to serve to an honored guest – it is not nullified. And the entire stringency of a “piece fit to serve to an honored guest” applies on condition that the piece is forbidden in itself, like non-kosher meat, or meat that was cooked with milk. But if it became forbidden because it absorbed forbidden flavor, for example it was cooked with non-kosher gravy, since the forbidden substance itself is not fit to serve to an honored guest, the law of the piece is like that of other forbidden substances (SA and Rema 101:2). If the pieces were cut until they are no longer fit to serve to an honored guest, the forbidden substance once again becomes nullified like other forbidden substances (SA 101:6).

sections.title: It Is Forbidden to Nullify Forbidden Substances
sections.html:
It is forbidden to nullify forbidden substances, whether by mixing nevela gravy into kosher gravy that is sixty times greater than it, or by mixing a piece of nevela meat with two kosher pieces like it. For since the Torah forbade eating them, it is forbidden to bring about a situation in which they will be nullified in a majority or in sixty and be eaten contrary to the intent of the Torah. Even if nevela gravy already became mixed into kosher gravy that did not contain sixty times against it, it is forbidden to add more water in order to nullify it in sixty. Likewise, if a piece of nevela meat and a piece of kosher meat became mixed, it is forbidden to add another permitted piece in order to nullify the forbidden substance in a majority. Likewise, if the mixture consisted of pieces fit to serve to an honored guest, or of especially significant items that are not nullified, it is forbidden to cut them up and cancel their significance so that the forbidden substance will be nullified in a majority or in sixty.

If one transgressed and nullified the forbidden substance: if he did so inadvertently – the forbidden substance is nullified. And if he did so intentionally – it is forbidden for him and for those for whom he did it to benefit from it, but for others the mixture is permitted (Mishna Terumot 5:9; Beitza 4b; Gittin 54b; SA 99:5).

However, if the forbidden substance that became mixed in is forbidden only by rabbinic law, and the kosher foods do not contain a sufficient quantity to nullify it, the Sages permitted adding to it in order to nullify it. Likewise, if it is a significant item that is not nullified – it is permitted to cut up the pieces in the mixture in order to nullify it (Rambam; SA 99:6). And some are stringent even when the prohibition is rabbinic (Rosh, Rema). And in a pressing situation, even those who follow their view may be lenient (Pri Megadim, Rabbi Akiva Eiger).

It is permitted to grind wheat intended for flour that has many insects mixed into it which are difficult to remove, and through the grinding the insects will be cut up and nullified in sixty. This is because the intent is not to nullify the forbidden substance but to grind the wheat into flour, and incidentally the forbidden substance is nullified (Taz 137:4).16

sections.title: Davar She-yesh Lo Matirin
sections.html:
A davar she-yesh lo matirin (something that will become permitted), that is, a forbidden food whose prohibition will lapse over time and it will become permitted, or that can be permitted through a simple action, which became mixed with its own kind – the Sages established that it is not nullified even in a thousand. Therefore, wheat that is forbidden under the prohibition of ḥadash (new grain before the omer offering) that became mixed with wheat from the previous year – even if the permitted wheat is a thousand times the forbidden, all of it is forbidden until the day of the omer, when the prohibition of ḥadash lapses. Likewise, produce of ma'aser sheni and hekdesh (consecrated property) that became mixed with other produce is not nullified, since it can be permitted by redeeming it with money (Nedarim 58a).

This is because the whole matter of nullifying forbidden substances in a majority or in sixty is be-di'avad, when one is forced to decide the status of the mixture; but if the forbidden substance is about to become permitted, whether through the passage of time or through an action that will permit it, instead of overpowering it by force and nullifying it, one should wait until it becomes permitted. All this is on condition that the forbidden substance is still noticeable in our awareness, that is, it became mixed with its own kind, and then, even though there is sixty times against it, the forbidden substance has not changed and its name remains as it was. But if the davar she-yesh lo matirin became mixed with a different kind, and there is sixty times against it, it is nullified by virtue of its extreme smallness, for its name and its flavor have vanished from the world, and therefore there is no need to wait until it becomes permitted (SA 102:1).

A rabbinic prohibition that will become permitted is also not nullified. Therefore, an egg laid on Yom Tov, which is forbidden as muktzeh until the conclusion of Yom Tov, that became mixed with a thousand eggs – all the eggs are forbidden until the conclusion of Yom Tov (Beitza 4b).

If by the time the permitted time arrives the flavor of the food will be spoiled, it is not considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin. But if it will deteriorate a little, in a manner that is not very noticeable, the forbidden substance is considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin and is not nullified (SA 102:4; Kreti 12).

If a utensil that absorbed forbidden flavor became mixed up with permitted utensils, since there is effort involved in performing hagala on all the utensils, it is not considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin. However, one should wait until a full day passes over the utensil that absorbed the forbidden substance, for then its flavor will be spoiled and by Torah law there will be no prohibition in it (Rashba; SA 102:3). And if they can easily be kashered by hagala, some say that even after a full day one must permit them through hagala (Shakh 8, based on the Maharil).17

sections.title: Ḥatikha Na'aseit Nevela (ḤaNaN) with Meat and Milk
sections.html:
When milk became mixed with meat and was cooked with it, both became entirely forbidden, that is, the entire piece became forbidden, and in the language of the Sages: ḥatikha na'aseit nevela (“the piece becomes nevela”), abbreviated ḤaNaN. For example, if 10 ml (milliliters) of milk fell onto a piece of meat of 90 ml, since the milk imparted flavor to the meat, the entire piece, which now measures 100 ml, becomes nevela. Therefore, if this piece fell into a meat dish of five liters, the entire dish becomes forbidden, because one does not calculate the milk alone; rather, the entire piece, whose volume is 100 ml, is considered nevela, and since the dish does not contain sixty times more than it, but only fifty times – all of it becomes forbidden. If those five liters that became nevela fell into a huge meat dish whose volume is 250 liters, all of it becomes forbidden, since it contains only fifty times against the five liters that became nevela. Thus those 10 ml of milk rendered forbidden, through a gradual process, a quantity of meat 25,000 times greater than themselves. If those 250 liters of meat were mixed into 250 pots, a liter into each pot, with each pot containing 50 liters of meat, all the mixtures became forbidden. Thus those 10 ml of milk rendered forbidden a quantity of meat 1,250,000 times greater than themselves. In this way one could continue and render forbidden all the meat that exists in the world, for as long as the mixture does not contain sixty times more than the forbidden substance, the entire mixture becomes forbidden and turns into an entirely forbidden substance. But if from the start, the first time, the meat had contained sixty times the 10 ml of milk that fell into it, the milk would have been nullified in sixty, and all these mixtures would have been kosher.

One can learn a moral idea from this halakha: as long as one does not succeed in nullifying evil, one should distance oneself from it, for otherwise it can corrupt and render everything forbidden through a gradual process. However, the distancing is for a short time, for over time the forbidden food deteriorates and its flavor becomes spoiled, and it can no longer render forbidden.18

sections.title: Ḥatikha Na'aseit Nevela (ḤaNaN) with Other Forbidden Substances
sections.html:
It is agreed that when meat became mixed with milk through cooking, the entire piece becomes nevela, for the meat alone is kosher, and the milk alone is kosher, and through their being mixed both became forbidden; thus the entire piece becomes nevela by Torah law, and if it falls into another dish that does not contain sixty times against it, the entire dish becomes forbidden. But the Rishonim disagreed regarding other forbidden substances that became mixed into kosher foods. For example, if 10 ml (milliliters) of blood became mixed into 90 ml of kosher meat, it is clear that the piece of meat mixed with blood is forbidden to eat; the question is whether it is considered nevela.

Some say that although the meat is forbidden to eat because of the blood mixed in it, it did not become nevela; therefore, if this forbidden piece of meat falls into another dish of 1,000 ml (a liter), since there is more than sixty times the forbidden blood there – the dish is kosher. However, the piece itself that originally absorbed the blood is forbidden, because it is possible that the blood remained in it and did not spread throughout the dish (Rabbeinu Efrayim, Rosh, SA 92:4).

And some say that the Sages made the laws of other forbidden substances the same as the law of meat and milk, and established that with other forbidden substances, too, ḥatikha na'aseit nevela; and since the blood rendered the piece of meat forbidden, the entire piece of meat became nevela, and if it fell into a dish that does not contain sixty times it, the entire dish is forbidden (Rabbeinu Tam, Ramban, Ran and Rema).19

sections.title: The Rules of Kamma Kamma Batel and Ḥozer Ve-ni'or
sections.html:
A question arose regarding a case in which a forbidden substance fell into a permitted one and was nullified, and afterwards another forbidden substance fell into the permitted food, and the permitted food contains a sufficient measure to nullify it, but if we combine it with the first forbidden substance that was nullified before, the permitted food does not contain a sufficient measure to nullify them. According to the rule kamma kamma batel (“the first, the first is nullified”), the first forbidden substance was nullified and can no longer combine with the second forbidden substance, for whenever there was knowledge between the falling of the first forbidden substance and the falling of the second forbidden substance – they do not combine. This is because at the time the matter became known, the permitted overpowered the forbidden and nullified it, and it can no longer combine with a forbidden substance that falls afterwards. On the other hand, according to the rule ḥozer ve-ni'or (“it reawakens”), the first forbidden substance reawakens and combines with the forbidden substance that has now fallen into the mixture, and if the permitted food does not contain a sufficient quantity to nullify both of them together, the entire mixture is forbidden.

In a case where the combination of the forbidden substances imparts flavor, it is agreed in halakha that the mixture is forbidden. For example, if a little milk fell into meat and was nullified in sixty, and afterwards more milk fell into the same pot of meat, if the flavor of the milk is perceptible in the meat, the mixture is forbidden; thus the milk that fell first combines with the milk that fell later to render the mixture forbidden.

However, when the mixture is min be-mino, and consequently the forbidden flavor is not perceptible in the mixture, the poskim disagreed about how to act. In practice, as long as all the forbidden substances together are not enough to render the mixture forbidden by Torah law – kamma kamma batel. But when the combination of the forbidden substances creates a Torah prohibition, the permitted food no longer has the power to nullify the forbidden substance that became mixed in it, and everything that was already nullified reawakens, and the mixture becomes forbidden (Pri Ḥadash 99:21; Gra 11).

For example, if soup of tereifa meat fell into soup of kosher meat, by Torah law, as long as the kosher is the majority, the mixture is kosher; however, the Sages enacted that only if the permitted contains sixty times against the forbidden is the mixture kosher (above halakha 2). Thus, if the kosher soup contained sixty times against the non-kosher, the mixture is kosher. And if again a measure of less than one sixtieth of non-kosher fell there, it too is nullified in sixty, and so again and again, as long as the matter became known between one falling and the next. Not only that, but the non-kosher that was nullified combines with the permitted, so that if more non-kosher soup falls there, and only together with the non-kosher that was nullified earlier does the soup contain sixty times against the new non-kosher, the mixture is kosher. But if the situation reaches the point that in practice half the soup is non-kosher, all the forbidden substances once again combine with one another, and the mixture is forbidden.20

sections.title: Forbidden Substances That Nullify One Another
sections.html:
If there was a kosher dish of 59 ml (milliliters), and one ml of ḥelev or one ml of blood fell into it, since the dish does not contain sixty times against the forbidden substance, the dish becomes forbidden. But if both fell into the dish together – a ml of ḥelev and a ml of blood – the dish is kosher, because the ml of ḥelev combines with the 59 kosher ml to nullify the blood, and the ml of blood combines with the 59 kosher ml to nullify the ḥelev. For a forbidden substance renders the mixture forbidden when it imparts flavor to it, and when there is sixty times against it, it cannot impart flavor; and since the flavors of the two forbidden substances differ from each other, neither of them can impart forbidden flavor to the rest of the mixture, which is sixty times greater than it (Rosh; SA 98:9).

But if the flavor of the two forbidden substances was the same and different from the dish, such as one ml of ḥelev and one ml of nevela fat that fell into 59 ml of a vegetable dish, since the flavor of the ḥelev and of the nevela fat is the same, they have the power to impart flavor to the dish, and it becomes forbidden. But if they fell into 59 ml of kosher fat, since the flavor of the forbidden substance is like the flavor of the permitted, they do not impart flavor to it, and the mixture is kosher. Let us explain further: by Torah law, whenever the forbidden substance does not impart flavor to the permitted, it is nullified in a majority. But since this is a liquid mixture, the Sages enacted that the forbidden substance is nullified only in sixty; and since these are two different forbidden substances, they nullify one another: the ml of ḥelev combines with the 59 ml of kosher fat to nullify in sixty the ml of nevela fat, and the ml of nevela fat combines with the 59 ml of kosher fat to nullify in sixty the ml of ḥelev (Tevu'ot Shor, Rabbi Akiva Eiger).
